triage.name: Penicillin allergy
triage.reason: Very common clinical problem with a clear history-based assessment (timing, symptoms, reaction type) and important implications for antibiotic choice.

review_issues: auto-repaired: labs: dropped 'tryptase' (not in the reference table)

age.peak: any age; most commonly reported in adults

demographics: Reported in about 10% of the general population, but fewer than 1 in 10 of those reports are confirmed by testing
More commonly reported in adults than children
More common in people with frequent antibiotic exposure or healthcare contact

risk_factors.text: Prior reaction to a penicillin or another beta-lactam antibiotic
Atopic disease such as asthma, eczema or allergic rhinitis

family_history: Penicillin allergy in a parent or sibling
Other drug allergies in the family

chief_complaints.text: I was told I'm allergic to penicillin
I broke out in a rash after taking amoxicillin
My face and lips swelled up after an antibiotic
I had trouble breathing after a penicillin shot

hpi.onset: Symptoms begin within minutes to hours after the dose in immediate reactions, or days to weeks after starting the drug in delayed reactions
hpi.duration: Immediate reactions last minutes to hours; delayed rashes can last days to weeks
hpi.progression: Immediate reactions can progress quickly from itching and rash to swelling, wheezing and low blood pressure; delayed reactions evolve over days and may spread
hpi.location: Skin is most often involved, especially the trunk, arms and legs; swelling can affect the face, lips, tongue or throat
hpi.quality: Itchy raised rash, hives, or swelling of the skin and soft tissues
hpi.severity: Ranges from mild itching and a few hives to severe breathing difficulty and collapse
hpi.timing: Tied to the antibiotic dose; immediate reactions occur within 1–6 hours, delayed reactions after 1–14 days
aggravating: Re-exposure to penicillin or a related beta-lactam

associated_symptoms.text: Swelling of the face, lips or tongue

pertinent_negatives: No reaction when the antibiotic was taken in the past
No chronic rash or hives unrelated to drugs
No recent infection with fever and rash before the antibiotic

argues_against: Asthma exacerbation unrelated to the drug

positives.text: Swelling of the face, lips or tongue

atypical.how_it_differs: Children often have a mild maculopapular rash with amoxicillin, especially when they have a viral illness such as Epstein-Barr virus; this is frequently not a true allergy.
Older adults may have had a reaction many years ago and cannot recall the details; the history is often vague and the risk of a true reaction is lower.
Pregnancy can be associated with new rashes and itching, which may be confused with a drug reaction; true penicillin allergy does not change with pregnancy but management of antibiotics differs.
missing_classic_features: Clear relationship to the antibiotic dose

atypical.how_it_differs: Immunocompromised patients may have blunted allergic responses, so severe reactions can be less obvious, and infections can mimic drug reactions.

general.mild: Comfortable, no distress; may have itching or a few hives
general.moderate: Uncomfortable, scratching, visible rash or swelling but no respiratory or circulatory compromise
general.severe: Anxious and distressed, with facial or airway swelling, wheezing or hoarseness
general.critical: Toxic or moribund, pale, diaphoretic, hypotensive, with altered mental status

Inspect the skin over the trunk and extremities
Inspect and palpate the face, lips, tongue and periorbital area
findings.finding: Non-pitting swelling of the lips, tongue, eyelids or face

findings.finding: Peeling or sloughing of the skin

findings.maneuver: Inspect the oral, ocular and genital mucosae
findings.finding: Painful erosions or ulcerations of the mucous membranes

findings.maneuver: Inspect the skin over the trunk, arms and legs

findings.finding: Normal blood pressure without orthostatic change

findings.maneuver: Inspect and palpate the face, lips, tongue and periorbital area
findings.finding: No swelling of the face, lips or tongue

findings.maneuver: Inspect the oral, ocular and genital mucosae

labs.caveat: Mild eosinophilia can accompany a drug reaction but is nonspecific; marked eosinophilia with rash and organ involvement suggests DRESS.
Leukocytosis is not expected in uncomplicated urticaria; consider infection or a severe systemic drug reaction.
Rises in drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) or interstitial nephritis.
Transaminitis suggests a systemic delayed drug reaction such as DRESS.
Nonspecific; may be elevated in a severe systemic drug reaction or in the infection being treated.

findings.finding: Nonspecific ST-T changes with hypotension or poor perfusion

findings.text: Usually normal; no infiltrate in anaphylaxis or isolated drug rash
Hyperinflation with flattened diaphragms when there is severe bronchospasm

initial.why: Looks for eosinophilia or leukocytosis suggesting a systemic drug reaction rather than a simple rash
Assesses renal function if a severe delayed reaction or dehydration is suspected
Detects penicillin-specific IgE in a patient with a history of an immediate reaction; must be done with the major and minor determinants plus histamine and saline controls
initial.only_if: history of an immediate reaction (urticaria, angioedema, wheezing or hypotension within 1–6 hours of a dose) and the patient is not currently reacting

initial.why: Increases sensitivity over skin prick testing for IgE-mediated penicillin allergy
initial.only_if: skin prick testing is negative and the history suggests an immediate reaction

initial.why: Alternative when skin testing is not available or is contraindicated

confirmatory.why: The reference standard: a graded oral challenge confirms or excludes penicillin allergy when skin testing is negative or when the history is low risk
confirmatory.only_if: skin testing is negative, or the history is low risk (reaction more than 10 years ago, unknown or non-urticarial rash, no severe features) and the patient is not currently reacting

supporting.why: Occasionally used to evaluate a delayed eczematous or contact reaction to a beta-lactam

not_indicated.why: Not needed for an isolated drug rash or uncomplicated urticaria; order only if pneumonia or another pulmonary process is suspected
Not part of routine evaluation; only useful during an acute severe reaction
Nonspecific and does not change management
Does not distinguish a drug reaction from infection reliably in this setting
Not relevant unless a secondary skin infection is suspected

decision_points: Confirm the reaction history: timing after the dose, symptoms, and whether it was immediate (minutes to hours) or delayed (days to weeks)

Do not skin test or challenge a patient who is currently reacting or who has a history of a severe reaction such as anaphylaxis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, DRESS or interstitial nephritis
Skin testing and challenge should be done where resuscitation equipment and trained staff are available
A negative skin test followed by a negative oral challenge allows the penicillin allergy label to be removed
For a patient with a severe reaction history, avoid penicillins and choose an alternative class rather than testing

differential.name: Viral exanthem
differential.why_considered: A maculopapular rash appearing during antibiotic treatment is often caused by the viral illness being treated, especially in children.

history: Rash appears with or shortly after fever and other viral symptoms
Rash is not clearly tied to the timing of the antibiotic dose
Similar rash occurred with a different antibiotic or without antibiotics
Sick contacts or a known viral illness
exam: Diffuse maculopapular rash without hives or swelling

differential.name: Anaphylaxis
differential.why_considered: Penicillin is a common trigger of anaphylaxis, and the same exposure can cause a mild rash or a life-threatening reaction.
differential.trigger: Hypotension, airway swelling, or severe bronchospasm after a penicillin dose

history: Symptoms begin within minutes of the dose
Rapid progression over minutes to an hour
Feeling faint, throat tightness, or difficulty breathing
labs: No routine lab confirms it; serum tryptase may be elevated during the acute event

differential.name: Stevens-Johnson syndrome / toxic epidermal necrolysis
differential.why_considered: A severe delayed drug reaction that can begin with a rash and fever after starting an antibiotic.
differential.trigger: Painful skin, blistering, or mucosal erosions after starting a drug

history: Rash begins 1–3 weeks after starting the drug
Skin pain and a burning sensation
Fever and malaise
Mouth, eye, or genital sores
exam: Erosions of the oral, ocular, or genital mucosae
labs: Elevated transaminases and creatinine in severe cases

differential.name: DRESS syndrome
differential.why_considered: A delayed drug reaction with rash, fever, and organ involvement that can be mistaken for a simple penicillin rash.
differential.trigger: Rash with fever, facial swelling, and eosinophilia 2–8 weeks after starting a drug

history: Rash begins 2–8 weeks after starting the drug
Fever and malaise
Facial swelling

differential.name: Chronic spontaneous urticaria
differential.why_considered: Recurrent hives can be mistaken for a drug reaction, especially when the patient is taking antibiotics.

history: Hives occur without antibiotic exposure
Recurrent episodes over weeks to months
No clear relationship to a dose
exam: Urticaria without angioedema or respiratory symptoms

differential.name: Infectious mononucleosis
differential.why_considered: A maculopapular rash after amoxicillin is common in Epstein-Barr virus infection and is often mislabeled as penicillin allergy.

history: Sore throat, fever, and fatigue before the rash
Rash appears after starting amoxicillin
Sick contacts
labs: Positive heterophile antibody or EBV serology

differential.name: Serum sickness-like reaction
differential.why_considered: A delayed reaction with rash, fever, and joint pain that can follow antibiotic exposure.

history: Rash begins 1–3 weeks after starting the drug
Fever and joint pain
No mucosal involvement

severity.mild: Itching or a few hives without swelling, breathing difficulty, or low blood pressure; the patient is comfortable and stable.
severity.moderate: Widespread urticaria or a maculopapular rash with facial or lip swelling but no airway compromise or hypotension.
severity.severe: Airway swelling, wheezing, or hoarseness with normal blood pressure, or a severe delayed reaction with skin pain, blistering, or mucosal erosions.
severity.critical: Anaphylaxis with hypotension, poor perfusion, or altered mental status; or toxic epidermal necrolysis with extensive skin detachment.

red_flags.finding: Hypotension or feeling faint after a penicillin dose
red_flags.meaning: Anaphylaxis; give epinephrine and call for help immediately
Upper airway swelling; risk of complete airway obstruction

red_flags.finding: Diffuse wheezing or shortness of breath
Skin pain, blistering, or mucosal erosions
red_flags.meaning: Stevens-Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis; stop the drug and admit

red_flags.finding: Fever, facial swelling, and eosinophilia weeks after starting the drug
red_flags.meaning: DRESS syndrome; stop the drug and evaluate for organ involvement

complications.name: Anaphylaxis
clues: Symptoms within minutes of the dose

special_populations.differences: Mild maculopapular rashes with amoxicillin are common, especially with viral infections such as Epstein-Barr virus, and are often not true allergy; many children can be delabeled after evaluation.
Reactions are often remote and poorly recalled; the risk of a true reaction is lower, but severe delayed reactions can still occur.
Penicillin allergy limits antibiotic options for conditions such as syphilis and group B streptococcus; skin testing and challenge can be done safely in pregnancy when indicated.
Allergic responses may be blunted, and infections can mimic drug reactions; a low threshold for evaluation is needed.

key_questions.question: What exactly happened when you took the penicillin or amoxicillin?
key_questions.looking_for: A specific description of the reaction: hives, rash, swelling, breathing trouble, or just nausea or diarrhea

key_questions.question: How soon after the dose did the symptoms start?
key_questions.looking_for: Within 1–6 hours suggests an immediate, IgE-mediated reaction; days to weeks suggests a delayed reaction

key_questions.question: How long ago did the reaction happen?
key_questions.looking_for: More than 10 years ago lowers the chance that the allergy is still present

key_questions.question: How was the reaction treated, and did it go away on its own or with medicine?
key_questions.looking_for: Needed epinephrine, an emergency visit, or hospitalization suggests a more severe reaction

key_questions.question: Have you taken any penicillin or related antibiotic since then?
key_questions.looking_for: Tolerating a later course makes a true allergy much less likely

key_questions.question: What other antibiotics or medicines have you taken without a problem?
key_questions.looking_for: Tolerance of cephalosporins or other beta-lactams lowers the risk of a cross-reactive allergy

key_questions.question: Have you ever had a reaction to a cephalosporin, carbapenem, or other antibiotic?
key_questions.looking_for: Multiple beta-lactam reactions raise concern for a true class-wide allergy

key_questions.question: Do you have hives, swelling, or trouble breathing right now?
key_questions.looking_for: Any current airway swelling, wheezing, or hypotension means an acute reaction is in progress

key_questions.question: Have you ever had a reaction with skin pain, blistering, peeling, or sores in your mouth or eyes?
key_questions.looking_for: Suggests Stevens-Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis; avoid all penicillins

key_questions.question: Have you ever had a reaction with fever, facial swelling, and feeling very unwell weeks after starting an antibiotic?
key_questions.looking_for: Suggests DRESS syndrome; avoid all penicillins

key_questions.question: Do you have asthma, eczema, or seasonal allergies?
key_questions.looking_for: Atopy is common but does not by itself confirm a drug allergy

key_questions.question: Does anyone in your family have a penicillin or other drug allergy?
key_questions.looking_for: Family history is a weak risk factor and does not change management

reasoning_points: The reaction history is the key step: timing after the dose separates immediate (minutes to hours) from delayed (days to weeks) reactions
Symptoms of hives, swelling, wheezing, or low blood pressure suggest an IgE-mediated immediate reaction
A mild maculopapular rash days after starting amoxicillin, especially in a child with a viral illness, is often not a true allergy
Gastrointestinal symptoms alone such as nausea or diarrhea are not a true allergy
A severe reaction history (anaphylaxis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, DRESS, or interstitial nephritis) means penicillins should be avoided
A low-risk history or negative skin testing can be followed by a graded oral amoxicillin challenge to remove the label
Removing an unconfirmed penicillin allergy label improves antibiotic choice and reduces resistant infections

easy: Adult who reports hives and lip swelling within an hour of a penicillin dose
Clear timing and clear symptoms of an immediate reaction
No current symptoms and no severe features
History is consistent and easy to classify
medium: Child with a maculopapular rash days after amoxicillin during a viral illness
Reaction happened more than 10 years ago and details are vague
Patient reports only nausea or diarrhea after penicillin
Patient has tolerated a cephalosporin since the reported reaction
hard: Older adult who cannot recall the reaction at all
Patient with a history of anaphylaxis who now needs a penicillin for syphilis or group B streptococcus
Multiple reported antibiotic allergies with unclear details
Pregnant patient needing a beta-lactam and the history is uncertain
Patient with a severe delayed reaction such as DRESS or Stevens-Johnson syndrome
